As we approach the Holiday Season, I think it is a good time to reflect
on the Bureau of Prisons' activities during the past year. Despite a number of
problerns and frustrations, I personally feel it has been a good year for the
organization. We opened four new institutions -- Lexington, Oxford, Pleasanton
and San Diego. This represents the first time in the history of the Bureau when
four institutions were opened during the course of one calendar year.
The Congress has continued to be responsive to our requests for
resources. While we are in a tight financial squeeze at the present time, I
think we can take heart in the fact that both the House and Senate Appropriations
Committee have demonstrated their confidence in the direction we are moving.
During the year, there were a number of important court decisions
affecting the Bureau of Prisons. From a personal standpoint, I was pleased
with the Fifth Circuit ruling on the Church of the New Song. In addition, the
Supreme Court followed our suggestions in both the McDonnell vs Wolff case
as well as in the Washington Post case.
Yesterday morning, J. J. Clark stopped by the office for a cup of coffee.
We discussed a number of items including the construction program, Functional
Unit Management, etc. J. J. was most complimentary of the changes he has
observed during the past year and commented on how far ahead the Bureau of
Prisons is in comparison with the rnany state and local institutions he has visited
since his retirement.
He was particularly complimentary of Functional Unit Management,
noting the many changes that have occurred at Petersburg since he served the
institution as warden. From time to time, it's good to get comments from
retirees who can provide a fresh perspective on what we are doing.
FINANCIAL PROBLEMS
In my discus sions with wardens and Regional Office staff, I am reminded
of the tight financial situation throughout the Bureau. By way of background, the
Congress originally approved the entire $169 million we requested for FY '75.
This amount was reduced by $5.2 million, however as a result of a recision in
overall federal spending. As a result of the recision, we are having a rough
year with no relief in sight.

there will be no additional funds available to supplement the

there also are areas such as overtime which can be managed effectively as
several wardens have demonstrated. I would appreciate any suggestions or
feedback you may have on our budgetary situation.
"THE FUTURE OF IMPRISONMENT"
Some of you have had the pleasure of rneeting Norval Morris, who is
Director of the Center for Studies of Criniinal Justice at the Univer sity of
Chicago Law School. Norval has recently written an excellent book entitled
t 1 The Future of Iinprisonrnent" which I believe should be required reading for
all the executive staff of the Bureau of Prisons. We are arranging to purchase
a copy of the book for each institution which will be sent to you within the next
several weeks.
I suggest you have all your top staff read the book am consider using
it in a staff discussion. As the attached review by Tom Wicker indicates, it's
a thought—provoking book which I think merits a great deal of consideration by
everyone in the field of corrections.
SPECIAL OFFENDERS
As you know, the concept of Special Offenders is currently under judicial
review at Danbury. We are appealing a recent decision of Judge Zampanot s
which I think would severely curtail our ability to identify and deal with the many
organized crime cases in our System. In this connection, several recent
incidents have been called to my attention where our staff have been recommending
parole in high level organized crime cases. As generally happens, these
particular inmates made excellent institutional adjustments and were able to
manipulate staff and, thus, receive a glowing recommendation to the Parole
Board.

We have recently received an unusually large number of letters and
phone calls from United States Attorneys, U. S. District Court Judges and
others concerning the overcrowded and inhumane conditions found in most
local jails.
Several weeks ago, the Chief Judges from the U. S. District Courts
in Maryland, Virginia and the District of Columbia met with Deputy Attorney
General Tyler and me to discuss their mutual concerns. All three districts
have trernendous problems in respect to housing inmates in the Inetropolitan
D. C.-BaItimore area. Despite the fact the new D. C. Jail opened last week,
it is already overcrowded and as a result, parts of the old jail will remain in
operation.
In follow-up to the concern expressed by the three judges, the Assistant
Directors and I met with Deputy Attorney General Tyler and Glen Pommerening
on Monday of this week. As a result of our discussions, the Department will be
submitting a budget amendment for FY 1977 to OMB requesting site and planning
funds for a Metropolitan Correctional Center in the D. C. area. Hopefully, such
a Center can be located near the Beltway around Washington, thus providing a
rapid access to all three District Courts -- Baltimore, Washington and
Alexandria.
In addition to discussing the jail situation in this area, we spent
considerable time reviewing other metropolitan areas where similar problems
exist. Emerging from our discussion was the decision that the Bureau will
consider building detention facilities in areas where the average federal caseload
exceeds 250.
In metropolitan areas where the population is not sufficient to justify a
separate facility, we are going to develop a legislative proposal which would
provide financial encouragement to state and local governments to include space
for federal inmates as they construct new jails and detention centers. I have
asked Sherm Day to work on this project in coordination with LEA A. Should
the proposal be accepted, it would undoubtedly be a responsibility that would
be assigned to the National Institute of Corrections. I know Sherm would
appreciate any suggestions or comments you might have.

the furlough program.
In this connection, I want to call your attention to the new Furlough
Policy Statement 7300. 121) which was issued on March 19. I urge you to
discuss the revised policy with your staff in order to insure that everyone
understands the changes that have been made. Of particular concern is the
absolute requirement for contact with the U. S. Probation Office to insure
consultation when a furlough is first being considered. This must be
accomplished by the use of the standardized form which has been developed
and is attached to the new Policy Statement.
UNFORTUNATE INCIDENTS
While I dislike singling out any institution in my comments, I am
attaching a recent article concerning a homosexual rape at Petersburg. My
reason for doing so in this case is that the incident could easily have occurred
in any of our institutions.
Incidents of this type call attention to the need for staff to be alert to
the possibility of transferring inmates who are obviously unsuited for an
institution because of age and/or physical appearance. When inmates are
committed that would more appropriately be handled in another institution, staff
should irnmediately telephone the Population Management Section here in the
Central Office and request an immediate redesignation rather than proceeding
with the time consuming referral process to effect a transfer. Once such

Again, I want to emphasize the importance for wardens to carefully

During our last meeting, the Executive Staff and I discussed the Task

increase of 179 since my last Director's Letter. One of the contributing
factors in the rise in population is a decline in the number of paroles.
The Parole Board recently made a comparison of changes in the type
of offenders being considered for parole during two time periods -- October
1974 to May 1975 and June 1975 to June 1976. The results of this comparison,
as reflected in the attached chart, indicate there have been a marked rise in
the number of offenders in the higher severity categories. The number of

inmates serving sentences for "moderate" offenses dropped from 497 to 399
while the number in the ' 'very highti category increased from 896 to 964. This
obviously indicates that the number of inmates incarcerated for more serious
offenses has been increasing. Such offenders will serve more time because of
the sentences imposed as well as the Parole Board's guidelines.
Yesterday, Dr. John Flanagan of the University of Wisconsin met with
us and discussed his projections for future prison populations. You may recall
that Dr. Flanagan wrote the article in the November -December is sue of the
Journal of Corrections which was circulated to all institutions.
Based on Dr. Flanagan's analysis, he predicts that the federal prison
population will continue to increase until reaching a peak of 35, 000 in 1985.
While such a figure staggers my imagination, the pos sibility certainly exists
that this projection may be accurate. As I have said before, things are going
to get worse before they get any better. The question is -
- how much worse?
PORNOGRAPHIC MOVIES
I was recently contacted by an Assistant U. S. Attorney who was
prosecuting a case involving interstate shipment of pornographic films. The
defendant in the case had alleged that the movies were .not pornographic and
stated that they had been shown in one of our major institutions. In checking
into the situation, we learned that although the producer had offered the film
free of charge, frie staff had wisely declined the offer.
I point this incident out as it again indicates how cautious we have to
be in accepting offers of 't free" movies or other forms of entertainment.
Without question, some of these individuals would like to put us in the t 'trick
bag", as they atter-npted to do in this instance and in a similar case some time
ago.

BEARDS
Without question, the most controversial item discussed by the Executive
Staff concerned policy on beards. As you know, the U. S. District Court in

incident reports on inmates who obviously make false statements in their
